column3: An ouroboros serpent (or a small Chinese dragon) whose scaled body IS the time: the digits are the path its body lies along, and the body is always sliding forward along that path (scales, a dorsal ridge, a head with a flickering tongue), so the time is never still. On the minute the head leaves the old glyph's path and slithers into the new one, the tail following and unwinding the old shape, one continuous motion. On the hour it sheds its skin: a hollow ghost skin of the old hour is left behind and crumbles away.

A glass furnace at night: the numerals are hot glass, pulled, coiled and pinched from glowing gathers on a blowpipe, and they cool while you watch (dithered heat glow fading to a dark outline with a bright rim, a heat shimmer above). On the minute the old digit is reheated in the glory hole until it slumps into a glowing gob, and the gaffer's tools pull and twist it into the new numeral. On the hour the furnace door swings open and floods the scene with orange light.

A cloud chamber in a magnetic field: charged particles leave condensation trails, straight muon streaks and curling electron spirals, that bloom, drift and fade as mist. The numerals are written by particle tracks (curling spirals, kinked tracks, V-shaped decays) so the strokes themselves look like physics. Stray cosmic rays keep the chamber alive every second; on the minute a burst of tracks wipes the old digit as it evaporates and the new digit condenses out of the mist. Keep it legible: the digit tracks must be bold and sustained, stray tracks rare and thin.

A Calder mobile hanging from the top edge: thin wire arms balanced at pivots, each carrying a flat sheet-metal plate cut in the shape of a numeral (organic, Calder-like cut-outs, not a font), slowly turning in 3D so plates go edge-on and swing back, and gently swaying. On the minute a new plate is hung, the arm's balance point shifts and the whole mobile rebalances with a damped, physically believable swing. On the hour a gust sends everything spinning before it settles.

A playful octopus in a dark rock pool whose tentacles curl into the numerals, suckers along their undersides, the tips always curling and tasting; its big expressive eyes watch the time. On the minute the arms involved uncurl, wave and re-coil into the new digit with springy, eased motion; it blinks, and maybe a little fish swims by. On the hour it squirts an ink cloud that blooms and clears to reveal the new hour. Carefully hand-drawn, cute, character-driven.

A troupe of tiny circus acrobats whose bodies are the strokes of the numerals: stacked, hand-to-hand, in arches and pyramids, wobbling to keep balance and breathing, never frozen. On the minute the acrobats in the changing digit somersault, flip and tumble into the new formation along eased arcs. On the hour a trapeze artist swings in or a human cannonball flies across. Hand-drawn sprite figures with personality, interacting with the time.

A popcorn machine: kernels sizzle in a kettle and pop with a jump into fluffy puffs that land and pile into the numerals (each puff a hand-drawn little cloud, the digits look made of popcorn). Pops keep happening every second, puffs settle and jiggle. On the minute the kettle tips and the old digit spills out, while fresh kernels pop and arc onto the new digit's shape. On the hour the lid blows off in a popping storm.

A Magic 8-Ball seen through its window: a floating icosahedron die drifts in dark blue liquid, bobbing and slowly rotating in real 3D, and its upturned triangular face carries the time in embossed letterforms designed for a triangle. Bubbles rise, the liquid has dithered depth. On the minute the ball is shaken: the die tumbles, its old face sinking away into the murk while a new face rolls up and presses to the glass. On the hour a big shake with a vortex of bubbles. Lay out hours and minutes so they read naturally on the die's faces.
